title: Event loop: tasks, microtasks, rendering steps, and the 50 ms task cap
summary: How the browser interleaves your JS, rendering, and input on a single thread — what runs in what order, why microtasks can starve the loop, and what `scheduler.yield()` and Long Animation Frames have to do with INP.
crux: One thread, two queues, one render step — and a 50 ms cap on whoever holds the floor.
keytakeaway: One thread, two queues, one render step. Microtasks drain before rendering — so awaiting a Promise is not a yield. Tasks longer than 50 ms blow up INP. Yield with `scheduler.yield()` or `setTimeout(0)`, never with `await Promise.resolve()`.

title: Render pipeline: parse → CSSOM → layout → paint → composite
summary: Six pipeline stages, who owns each thread, what triggers each invalidation, and how to read a DevTools flame strip to find the bottleneck.

keytakeaway: Six stages, two threads. Animate transform and opacity, not top and width. Batch reads before writes. The frame budget after browser overhead is ~10 ms — that decides everything.

title: V8 internals: tiered JIT, hidden classes, inline caches, and Orinoco GC
summary: Inside the four-tier JIT pipeline (Ignition + Sparkplug + Maglev + TurboFan), hidden-class polymorphism, inline-cache states, deoptimization, and Orinoco's concurrent garbage collector.
crux: V8 = 4 JIT tiers + hidden classes + ICs + Orinoco GC. Polymorphism above 4 shapes kills hot paths 10-50x.
keytakeaway: V8 perf = stable hidden classes + monomorphic ICs + no deopt-loops + low GC pressure. Break any one and a hot loop loses 10-50x. Fix at code shape, not at V8 flags.

title: Workers: web workers, service workers, worklets, and SharedArrayBuffer
summary: Four ways to run code off the main thread — web workers (compute), service workers (network proxy), worklets (render-thread hooks), SharedArrayBuffer (shared memory) — with the structured-clone cost, COOP/COEP gates, and lifecycle traps.
crux: Thread or proxy: web workers compute, service workers proxy the network, worklets hook rendering, SharedArrayBuffer shares memory.
keytakeaway: Four off-main-thread tools, four jobs: web workers offload compute, service workers proxy the network, worklets hook the render pipeline, SharedArrayBuffer shares memory. None touch the DOM. `postMessage` deep-copies by default — transfer large buffers. SharedArrayBuffer needs COOP + COEP or it is `undefined`.

title: React Fiber: the reconciler, render vs commit, lanes, and time-slicing
summary: How React turns a tree of components into DOM mutations — the fiber unit of work, the double-buffered tree, the interruptible render phase, the atomic commit phase, priority lanes, and the 5 ms time-slice that keeps input responsive.
crux: A tree of components becomes DOM mutations: render computes the diff (interruptible), commit applies it (atomic).
keytakeaway: Two phases: render builds the workInProgress tree and is interruptible; commit applies DOM mutations and is atomic. Fibers store state, so a key change destroys it — use stable ids, never the index. Lanes prioritise; `startTransition` keeps a heavy render from blocking input. Referential stability is what lets a fiber bail out.

title: Render strategies: SSR, SSG, ISR, streaming, RSC — and the cost of hydration
summary: When to render the HTML — per request (SSR), at build (SSG), on demand (ISR), in chunks (streaming) — and what hydration costs to turn that static HTML into a live app: full vs selective vs progressive vs islands vs resumability.
crux: SSR, SSG, ISR, streaming — *when* to render the HTML. Hydration — the price to make that HTML interactive.
keytakeaway: SSG renders at build, SSR per request, ISR refreshes static on a schedule, streaming flushes the shell first. Hydration is the separate, ~2× cost of making that HTML interactive. Cut it: Server Components ship no client code, islands hydrate only interactive parts. Keep renders deterministic or hydration mismatches flash and shift the page. Choose per route.

title: Core Web Vitals: LCP, INP, CLS — what each measures and what causes it
summary: The three field metrics Google scores a page on — Largest Contentful Paint, Interaction to Next Paint, Cumulative Layout Shift — what counts toward each, the lab-vs-field gap, and how to read a DevTools trace to find the cause.
crux: Three field metrics: did it show up fast (LCP), does it respond (INP), does it stay still (CLS)?
keytakeaway: Three field metrics at p75: LCP ≤2.5 s (did it show up), INP ≤200 ms (does it respond), CLS ≤0.1 (does it stay still). LCP splits into four phases — fix the dominant one. INP splits into input delay, processing, presentation — early-only INP is hydration. CLS is un-sized late content — reserve space. Debug in the lab, judge in the field.
